Arikara

Arikara, or Sahnish, is a distinct people within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation. This reviewed starting guide covers village histories, river-community displacement and educational priorities. Deeper Arikara-specific research remains unfinished.

Names & relationshipsArikara/Sahnish is a distinct people within the shared Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation. Mandan and Hidatsa are allied constituent peoples, not aliases for Arikara. Fort Berthold is a reservation and governmental context, not the entirety of historical homelands. The three languages and Arikara-specific educational work require separate attention.
A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

This pass refreshes six original access points and supplies a carefully scoped orientation from three substantive explanatory works, with three short supporting references. Initial adequacy is not yet established. Direct Sahnish-authored scholarship, actual language-learning publications, fuller historical primary records and contemporary Arikara-specific perspectives remain insufficient. An index or short contextual introduction cannot fill those gaps.

Assessment recorded October 21, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The historical Nation page was inspected through its actual indexed body after direct timeouts; its selected interpretation and date disagreement require further corroboration.
  • The language portal explains educational priorities, but no linked textbook, handout, dictionary, class recording or language study was actually read.
  • The chapter and NPS introduction offer useful outside orientation, not a complete history or community review. The substantive target of twelve is not reached.
01

A shared government and distinct peoples

MHA Nation’s official site identifies the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation at Fort Berthold in North Dakota. It describes a Tribal Business Council with a chairman and representatives from six segments. This provides institutional orientation to a shared government; it does not make Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara interchangeable names or turn the reservation into their entire historical homeland.

Read the sources [4] MHA Nation

02

Village movements and river-community displacement

MHA Nation’s history distinguishes Sahnish village movements from Mandan and Hidatsa histories. Its narrative and timeline differ between 1862 and 1863, so the move into Like-a-Fishhook is described here as the early 1860 s. The page also recounts Garrison Dam relocation as a loss of fertile bottomlands and connected communities, with relocation completed by fall 1954.

Read the sources [1] MHA Nation

03

Language priorities and community educational work

MHA Nation presents Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara as separate languages and acknowledges Elders, teachers, Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College and the MHA Language Project. Its portal identifies learning materials and past Arikara class recordings. This is an institutional account of educational priorities and collaboration; listing resources does not establish their contents, effectiveness or present class schedules as independently checked.

Read the sources [2] MHA Nation

04

Gardening and village economies

North Dakota Studies identifies Sahnish as the people’s own name and places Arikara village history along the Missouri River. Its educational account describes earthlodge homes, gardening of corn, beans and squash, food preservation and hunting. It also discusses epidemics and movement toward Like-a-Fishhook. These selected historical explanations do not describe every family or establish present practices.

Read the sources [3] North Dakota Studies / State Historical Society of North Dakota

05

Reading expedition accounts critically

The NPS introduction identifies Arikara as a Caddoan language and describes farming villages and regional trade. It explicitly warns that expedition observers’ accounts were not necessarily correct from Indigenous perspectives and that the displayed excerpts have been adapted. These limits matter: similar-looking homes do not establish common origins, and an edited excerpt is distinct from an original journal.

Read the sources [5] National Park Service / Gateway Arch National Park

06

A reconstruction used for public interpretation

The NPS visitor entry identifies the Earthlodge Village near New Town as a reconstruction managed by MHA Nation. Its interpretation concerns Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara peoples together. The listing offers an introduction to public historical interpretation, rather than an unchanged ancestral settlement or an exclusively Arikara village; present visitor arrangements require separate checking.

Read the sources [6] National Park Service

What needs further research

  • Read a substantial community-directed Arikara language textbook, dictionary introduction or documented educational study through legitimate public access, without reproducing narratives or audio.
  • Broaden direct Sahnish-authored accounts and historical scholarship; a shared-government overview cannot represent every constituent people’s experience.
  • Read actual primary records for village movement, colonial trade, treaties and dam displacement, preserving their period, authorship and community perspectives.
  • Corroborate the 1862/1863 movement chronology; do not resolve conflicting dates by pretending sources agree.
  • Verify present cultural/educational institutions separately, rather than converting undated descriptions or a 2021 visitor listing into current operations.
  • No community review, contemporary speaker census or assessment of learner outcomes has occurred.

Six original routes were rechecked; three substantive explanatory works and three supporting references are recorded. This is a reviewed starting guide, not an adequate deep-dive collection or a completion claim. The MHA history page was read through its actual indexed body after direct timeouts. Its internal 1862/1863 chronology difference is retained as uncertainty; page availability is not mislabeled a paywall. The language portal’s institutional explanation counts once. Underlying books, recordings, handouts and applications remain unread, and no audio was played. A linked Arikara Project access failure adds no work. The NPS expedition introduction is supporting; adapted excerpts are distinct from original journal editions. The short reconstructed-village listing concerns all three MHA peoples and is not an Arikara-specific architectural study.

MHA Nation History — selected Sahnish, village and relocation sections ↗

A substantial Nation-published historical account differentiates constituent peoples and describes village changes and dam-related displacement. Selected public historical sections are used; conflicting dates and outdated extinction language elsewhere are not silently adopted.

Inspection scope: Actual extended body rendered by exact-URL search: Arikara section, Historical overview, Village & Relocations, and Elbowoods/Fort Berthold relocation paragraphs. Direct opens timed out; no underlying manuscripts, origin narratives or linked books reviewed.
